newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Ousted Romania leader challenges winner on pledges.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Romania leader challenges winner on pledges.

text.p: Romania's defeated President Ion Iliescu challenged his successor Emil Constantinescu on Tuesday to make good on campaign pledges to speed reform and boost some of eastern Europe's lowest living standards.

Addressing his last news conference before academic Emil Constantinescu's inauguration this week, the ex-communist said his centrist opponents had won the presidency and control of parliament "by making left-wing promises".

"I think the major problem in the years to come for those in power will be reconciling the contradiction between election promises and economic realities," Iliescu said beneath two huge chandeliers in the Cotroceni presidential residence.
"The new government and the new president have made big promises. We preferred to lose the elections rather than promise things we knew we could not deliver."
Iliescu, in power since the 1989 overthrow of communism, lost to Constantinescu in last week's presidential run off.
The president-elect's centrist allies had won general elections two weeks earlier, running on a campaign to speed reform, liberalise markets and boost social benefits.
Iliescu's leftists were thrown out of government for the first time in seven years, but the outgoing president won a seat in parliament where he will now head the opposition.

Constantinescu is to be sworn in on Friday. Negotiations have been under way for a week on forming a government led by his Democratic Convention and including Social Democrats and members of the 1.6 million Hungarian minority.
In an 80-minute address to reporters, Iliescu said he had promulgated 663 laws in his last four-year term in office and fielded 124,000 requests and complaints from individuals.
He said Romania had become a "factor of stability" in eastern Europe, despite an even worse economic crisis in Bulgaria to the south and conflict in Yugoslavia to the West.
His country, he said, deserved to be in the first wave of NATO enlargement planned next year, but Romania is considered a long-shot after Hungary, the Czech Republic and Poland.
He told reporters his principal shortcoming had been the inability to form a pact between political parties to "weather the worst part of the transition to the market".
He also regretted poor relations with a hostile press, with most major dailies lined up against him in the campaign.
"As an element of self-criticism, I did not find the best way of dialogue with the press," he said.
